This is sad for higher education. 

Throughout history the best universities have been global hubs of science, philosophy, and innovation. In the Middle Ages, the University of Bologna, in Italy, was Europe’s most important university. It is estimated that in the 13th century it attracted students and scholars from all over Christendom, with well OVER 50% of students being foreign. When Oxford started to become a global hub of knowledge, it also started attracting international talent, by the eve of WWI it had around 10% of international students. Nowadays Oxford is around 23% international among undergrads, close to 45% considering the full student body. Cambridge sits at around 37%, National University Singapore is 39%, the Sorbonne is 23%.

The American average is around 5-6%, ivies sit at around 20%.

It is normal for global institutions at the forefront of knowledge creation to have international student bodies. Not even just normal, but mandatory. It is so tiring to hear the same argument that American universities are somehow in a unique position of exploitation where foreigners take advantage of their education. Every major university is internationalized, and it has been like thatfor a very long time.

If Americans want colleges to be local institutions without global ambitions, and without global impact, that’s fine; but be aware that that also means American colleges cannot continue to be at the forefront of knowledge and innovation.

comments.name: Frustrated Independent
comments.body: There is a lot of truth here. What I have not yet seen is an explanation of law firm economics. Law firm have enormous financial commitments — compensation guarantees, associate and staff salaries, long-term office leases, furniture/fixtures/equipment, and sharply increasing technology costs. A portion of these cost are financed through loans of various sorts, which have to be repaid. It does not take a very large reduction in revenue to have a material effect on the sufficiency of cash flow to meet these obligations, or to cause a breach of financial covenants on loan documents. While the “Greed” of free agency may get the ball rolling, it is the cash flow requirements and loan covenants that often lead to the difficult decision to dissolve, since the financial commitments can’t be “right-sized” fast enough to match reduced revenue. In the “good old days” the practice of law was less capital intensive and, thus, less financially leveraged.

They don't so much advertise as try to inveigle listeners into believing that just about anything that ever happened to them or to their family may be a sueable offense, and "you should get the settlement you deserve". Even if you initiated the total action, 'you may be entitled to a settlement', and then they give examples of monetary settlements of a million bucks for what you might have (actually rightly) perceived as a 10k case. They have people bending over backwards to find reasons for you to sue just about anybody over just about anything. It's all covered by the law, you know! When housing is purely seen as a commodity, there will be thousands of people (landlords, investors, not all of them fat cats) who are hurt and angry when the government tries instead to administer it as a right; when the hospitality industry has gotten used to a business model predicated on super low employee wages and prices, policies that raise those wages (and inevitably prices too) will ultimately put some restaurants out of business, and not all of them will have been run by ruthless plutocrats. Writing is not brilliance, as you write in the article. It’s work. Risk. Loneliness, personal strength. To write, one must be able to feel, so writing requires sensitivity. Writers are (like all humans) are injured in some way, which makes them sensitive and needy. They’ve usually been exposed to some book or other that maybe made them feel seen or understood. Or, they’ve experienced awe in reading. 

The myth of so-called brilliance in writers is based on the following physical reality: when one sits alone for long periods of time trying to come up with ideas, the subconscious and the conscious mind learn to communicate with each other on command. It feels and appears magical when a writer puts down the words to the ideas that form. However, this is simple computing. (Such is the devastation of giving our high school students “devices.” Some  can’t think deeply bc it requires silence and focus. The child’s mind can be trained easily, but it takes stretches of time combined with measurable outcomes, like math problem solutions or stories or observations about the world). 

Please, stop with the brilliance myth. As Toni Morrison clarified, it is an insult to artists and the insane amount of work they do to get the products they make. Art is WORK.

comments.name: eric l.
comments.body:
A mountainous problem in our relationships to Philip Roth is his contradictions.

So much of his writing and his stances in life--the concern about how to live properly, morally, courageously; the horror over Nixon, and over McCarthyism; the publication of the works of dissident writers behind the former Iron Curtain, etc., bespeak a life of remarkable commitment to honor, freedom, the pursuit of justice.

And then there are the tales of his conduct in later years: How when he lectured at colleges, his professor friends would make sure that the coeds most eligible for liaisons with Roth were seated in the front rows. His hard-to-forget quip, "What's the point of having an attractive young woman in the house if you're not going to f**k her?"

I know that we each contain multitudes; that we are living contradictions; that a male artist who creates beautifully rounded, somewhat feminine sculptures may prove to be an angry misogynist in his everyday life; that our inner drives are sometimes the opposite of our social presentations; that Roth's inner Portnoy was bound to emerge eventually, given the right opportunity.

Yet even given that knowledge, the contradictions within Philip Roth are particularly outstanding and disturbing.

My first Roth book was The Ghost Writer - I'd recommend it as a short beginning if you've not read him before. From Mr Foer, whose own writing also needs mentioning, and whose annotations on the Roth essay grow quietly before gathering pace, I'm glad I began with Everything is Illuminated.

comments.name: eric l.
comments.body:
When I was a child I experienced  fiction as make-believe that I had to suspend disbelief to relate to at all; not entirely more realistic than "The Knights of the Round Table".

Then at age 15 I borrowed Roth's "Good-bye, Columbus" from my parents' bookshelves. "The first time I saw Brenda she asked me to hold her glasses..."

And I thought "Holy Moses! This is EXACTLY  like real life."

For nearly a decade after, Roth's career failed to live up to that literary and popular triumph. "When She Was Good" and "Letting Go" were difficult, depressing books. Then in the spring of 1968 the first samples of what would be Portnoy began to appear in literary magazines. How could people not take notice of a chapter titled "Whacking Off"?!

In 1969 the entire Portnoy landed on America.

And from then on, the literary landscape was Philip Roth's oyster.

In any case, Sotheby's established that the Van Gogh sold for a very high price in 1936, significantly more than the Van Gogh from Paul Allen's collection (which sold for 117m in 2022) had sold for in 1935. I suppose you cannot quantify the effect that the Nazi regime had on the family's publishing business, but it seems telling that they made efforts to recover works that sold in 1938,  but not this painting. It would be interesting to hear why they are pursuing this work now, when they did not pursue the Cézanne offered at Christie's in 2007, nor have they ever made claims on an additional Cézanne that they also sold in 1936, which has been in the collection of the Harvard Art Museums for decades. I imagine that Sotheby's did not contact the family because of their lack of pursuit of these other works; the auction house was not working to hide the Fischer provenance on the website, as the painting has an unbroken line of provenance beginning with the artist's brother. In any case, this painting was not stolen by the Nazi's and smuggled to South America.

I would be more conciliatory about Noah Kahan’s snub if it wasn’t for the fact that Taylor Swift’s the Life of a Showgirl made the short list for AOTY…

Kahan pulls off a truly difficult task by making his “I’ve made it” album something that is still incredibly rooted in relatability. So much so, in fact, that Kahan’s most popular song from The Great Divide is about losing at the Grammys (Orbiter). A subject matter which could easily come off as out-of-touch or hubristic is instead made into a love letter about familial support and unconditional love. 

Taylor Swift, on the other hand, produced a truly vindictive and rudimentary record that even her most ardent fans refuse to defend. An album which seems less interested in exploring the duality of performance (as the album title suggests) and more interested in score-settling and “proving the haters wrong.” Including a gratuitous description of her new husband’s… wood (Wood).  

It is interesting that both of these albums take fame and celebrity as their centerpiece. But by elevating Swift’s self-aggrandizement over Kahan’s introspective humility, the Grammy voters reveal their own hubris.

A century ago, financial institutions demonstrated the risks inherent in unregulated financial systems. Glass-Steagall, the Securities acts of 1933 and 1934 and other legislation set firewalls between financial businesses and created regulatory systems that enabled the U.S. to grow the largest and most successful economy in the world. But! It is completely obvious- in publishing, in TV, film, these outreaches are "paid"- these agents and managers are being paid small fees to read your pitch, outline, treatment, book, script.  Of course they are.  And, considering as many professionals say- they know within 10 pages of a script whether they are interested or not- it's sustainable, if not profitable.  

On the one hand- it does bring new, unrepped talent in the mix, to even be glanced at.  It's exhausting to do pitch sessions - this can be done at one's own leisure. 

But- more obvious- and not the fault of these managers, etc- the buying market is unbearable tough now- it's very very hard to sell things to studios, publishers.  This is how a lot of managers, agents, make their own living now.  It's not a mystery. 

So- if you have a thick skin, and the money to pitch/submit- it's not entirely a bad idea.  It revolutionalizes the guardrails- you have to be clever and think outside the box. Neighbors burn high lumen floodlights all night long mounted on garages, barns, homes and rental mini storage units. Street lights too. Could it then have started gaining traction over time, slowly shifting people’s perception from ridicule and illusion to something real and desirable - especially once promoted by social media influencers and other service providers in the collectibles industry?

My guess is that these tradable cards are probably not as rare as masterpiece artworks occasionally sold through an official bidding process at auction houses. Personally, I am not familiar with this specific marketplace, but, in general, I tend to believe that sustaining a market would require steady and stable demand from willing and able buyers as well as a high enough volume of trades supported by transparent and readily available bid/ask prices. We are nearly always cast as interlopers looking to steal the affection of the female main character’s husband and/or child through emotional manipulation or even murder if necessary. Occasionally, we’re the naive twenty-something who (somehow) got a cushy nannying job in a large old manor house despite having no childcare experience to speak of. 

The reality is very different. Setting aside that any employer pursuing a relationship with their employee is a predator, doubly so if there’s a significant difference in age and wealth, these domestic cautionary tales simply don’t reflect what it means to be a nanny. 

Nannies play a unique role in the lives of young families and especially young children. We aren’t these kids’ parents, nor would we want to be (a nanny wanting a child of their own is something different.) We come to love the kids in our care, while knowing that there will come a day where we have to say goodbye, and it will always break our hearts even if we remain friends with the family.
